metadata.title: Oracle stock sinking as its AI spending climbs, debt grows

content.text:
Oracle (ORCL) stock has dropped by as much as 10% in Thursday's pre-market trading despite topping fiscal fourth quarter earnings and revenue estimates.
Morning Brief Host Julie Hyman is joined by Yahoo Finance Tech Editor Dan Howley and Monetary Matters Network co-founder Jack Farley for a conversation about whether the AI infrastructure company is showing signs of weakness or oversaturation in the buildout landscape.
So the company spending, um, for its last fiscal year, $55.7 billion. It's expected to be $70 billion in fiscal 2027, which is its current year. Now, everybody's spending a lot of money. We know, um, all these companies are spending a lot of money. We also know there has been concern around Oracle in particular. And Oracle is saying that it is going to raise about $20 billion in debt and equity financing in this, um, current fiscal year. It had already announced about $20 billion in equity issuance. So this is then on top of that. So, you know, Oracle is not exactly in the same position as some of these other tech companies in terms of of, um, cash they have on hand.
Yeah. They they I mean if you look at they're also not raising as much, obviously, right? I mean, if you look at something like Microsoft or Google or Amazon, they're raising, you know, in the the multi multi tens of billions, right? Hundreds of billions of dollars. I think it's what, 7 720 was 725 around there was the the total that they're expected to spend this year. By the way,
I think that's right. Yeah.
going up next year. Yes. So, if everything remains, you know, on the level. And yeah, I think for Oracle, obviously a lot of the the kind of concern is the fact that it's so tied up with Open AI. Right? They have that $300 billion five-year deal. There's been concern as to, you know, will Open AI be able to continue to pay for these kinds of buildouts? Can they continue to build out? Um and so they're, you know, they filed their S1 on uh Monday uh or confidentially. Uh and so, you know, I think for for Oracle in particular, it's it's that kind of lack of clarity as to who are your who are your big clients? How are you going to now recoup all And it feels as though it's almost taking like uh where we saw Microsoft, Google and Amazon at the beginning of this buildout, right? There was that whole, ooh, you guys are spending a lot of money. And then I think there was the the realization that, well, you guys also make a lot of money too. And oh, okay, you're starting to show us that that there's there's revenue being generated here. Your cloud uh services are are improving. Granted they were still on the upswing prior to AI. Um but this is, you know, additive to that. I think that's kind of where Oracle is at this moment. It's just that that heavy reliance on Open AI for that that huge deal. I think that continues to weigh on people.
Yeah.
Yeah.
I think on the debt side, it's interesting because unlike like other companies, they basically all the hyperscalers, Oracle does actually hover just above investment grade. So I think, you know, it has been a very indebted company, which is not true of Oracle, you know, Google has a positive cash cash position as do many of many of the other ones. It's

the the for the free cash flow was I was about negative about $60 billion last year and it's probably going to get a little bit more negative. So I think yeah, Oracle is definitely is the most company that's going to devour the most capital relative to its its revenue and and earnings. So I think the market is right to to be skeptical.
